# Batch 1 vs batch 2: YAP1C sulfenome findings

Comparison of [nucYAP1_batch1_analysis.Rmd](nucYAP1_batch1_analysis.Rmd) and
[nucYAP1_batch2_analysis.Rmd](nucYAP1_batch2_analysis.Rmd), from their written
outputs (`output_batch1/results`, `output_batch2/results`).

## Design difference

| | batch 1 | batch 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Runs | 16 (4 per group) | 12 (3 per group) |
| Reproducibility rule | 3 of 4 | 2 of 3 |
| Min possible Fisher p (3 vs 3) | 0.029 | 0.10 |

```{r design-check}
# The batch 2 sample sheet sets the floor on any 3-vs-3 detection test.
fisher.test(matrix(c(3, 0, 0, 3), nrow = 2))$p.value
```

## Global protein-group identifications

Before any interactor logic, how much of the proteome does each batch see, and
do the two probes see the same proteins? These counts come straight from the
DIA-NN report with the notebooks' own filter (target precursors at q <= 0.01 and
PG q <= 0.01 with a positive quantity), so a protein group counts as identified
in a run if it has at least one such precursor there. No replicate minimum is
applied — this is the raw observability behind the analysis.

```{r global-identifications}
# Per-run protein-group lists, one row per run x identified group.
pg_per_run <- function(batch) {
  base <- file.path("data", paste0("HL_nucYAP1_batch", batch), "DIA-NN_output")
  design <- readr::read_tsv(file.path(base, "experiment_design.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  arrow::read_parquet(file.path(base, "report.parquet"),
                      col_select = c("Run", "Protein.Group", "Q.Value",
                                     "PG.Q.Value", "Precursor.Quantity", "Decoy")) |>
    filter(Decoy == 0, Q.Value <= 0.01, PG.Q.Value <= 0.01, Precursor.Quantity > 0) |>
    distinct(Run, Protein.Group) |>
    inner_join(design, by = "Run") |>
    mutate(batch = batch)
}

pg_run <- bind_rows(pg_per_run(1), pg_per_run(2))

# Identifications per individual run: the spread within a batch is QC.
pg_run |>
  count(batch, Run) |>
  summarise(runs = n(), min = min(n), median = median(n), max = max(n), .by = batch)
```

Both probes see roughly the same number of protein groups within a batch, and
almost all of them are shared:

| Batch | YAP1A only | YAP1C only | Both probes | Union |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 137 | 635 | 4418 | 5190 |
| 2 | 169 | 165 | 1583 | 1917 |

```{r genotype-overlap}
genotype_counts <- function(batch) {
  d  <- filter(pg_run, batch == batch)
  ya <- unique(d$Protein.Group[d$Genotype == "YA"])
  yc <- unique(d$Protein.Group[d$Genotype == "YC"])
  tibble(batch = paste("batch", batch),
         YA_only = length(setdiff(ya, yc)),
         YC_only = length(setdiff(yc, ya)),
         both = length(intersect(ya, yc)),
         union = length(union(ya, yc)))
}
genotype_counts(1) |> bind_rows(genotype_counts(2))
```

The two batches overlap by less than a third of their combined lists, and the
difference is depth rather than identity of the proteins:

| | Batch 1 only | In both batches | Batch 2 only |
|---|---|---|---|
| Protein groups | 3573 | 1617 | 300 |

```{r batch-overlap}
u1 <- unique(pg_run$Protein.Group[pg_run$batch == 1])
u2 <- unique(pg_run$Protein.Group[pg_run$batch == 2])
tibble(batch1_only = length(setdiff(u1, u2)),
       in_both     = length(intersect(u1, u2)),
       batch2_only = length(setdiff(u2, u1)))
```

Reproduction across runs is the same shape in both batches, shifted by about
1500 groups:

| Protein groups seen in ... runs | batch 1 (16 runs) | batch 2 (12 runs) |
|---|---|---|
| 1-3 runs (sporadic) | 742 | 484 |
| 4-8 runs | 869 | 413 |
| 9-12 runs | 683 | 1020 |
| 13-16 runs | 2896 | 0 |

```{r replication}
pg_run |>
  count(batch, Protein.Group) |>
  mutate(seen = cut(n, breaks = c(0, 3, 8, 12, 16), labels = c("1-3", "4-8", "9-12", "13-16"))) |>
  count(batch, seen) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = batch, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

Two things follow for the rest of the comparison. Batch 1 is roughly 2.7x deeper
per run (2816-4304 groups vs 1013-1436 in batch 2), which is more than a
4-vs-3 replicate difference; and the batches share only 1617 protein groups, so
a protein that is "batch 1 only" may simply not be observable in batch 2 rather
than being absent from the sample.

## Scale of the results

| Step | batch 1 | batch 2 |
|---|---|---|
| YAP1C interactors (Step 1) | 3624 | 1237 |
| Route A: absent from YAP1A | 184 | 61 |
| Route B: enriched over YAP1A | 38 | 10 |
| Specific interactor set | 222 | 71 |
| Proteins quantified in both treatments | 99 | 26 |
| Detection-only proteins | 123 | 45 |

```{r counts}
n_counts <- function(batch) {
  c(interactors        = nrow(rd(batch, "YAP1C_all_interactors.csv")),
    route_a            = nrow(rd(batch, "unique_YAP1C_interactors.csv")),
    route_b            = nrow(rd(batch, "YAP1C_enriched_significant.csv")),
    specific           = nrow(rd(batch, "YAP1C_specific_interactors_broadened.csv")),
    both_arms          = sum(rd(batch, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_test_coverage.csv")$tested_in == "both arms"),
    detection_only     = sum(rd(batch, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_test_coverage.csv")$tested_in == "detection only"))
}
rbind(batch1 = n_counts(1), batch2 = n_counts(2))
```

Route B is narrow in both: 1053 of 3212 proteins pass the YAP1C-vs-YAP1A test at
adj. p < 0.05 in batch 1 (115 of 1264 in batch 2), but only 38 (batch 2: 10) also
clear the fold-change and specificity filters.

```{r route-b}
route_b_tested <- function(batch) {
  e <- rd(batch, "YAP1C_vs_YAP1A_limma.csv")
  c(tested = nrow(e), sig = sum(e$adj_pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))
}
rbind(batch1 = route_b_tested(1), batch2 = route_b_tested(2))
```

## High light vs normal light

Neither batch found a single protein whose **intensity** changed with
treatment (limma, adj. p < 0.05): 0 of 99 testable in batch 1, 0 of 26 in
batch 2. No protein passed the Fisher **detection** test either, and in batch 2
none could (smallest attainable p = 0.10 with 3 vs 3 replicates).

```{r hl-nl-tests}
for (b in 1:2) {
  d  <- rd(b, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_differential.csv")
  pa <- rd(b, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_presence_absence.csv")
  cat(sprintf("batch %d: intensity %d/%d significant at adj.p < 0.05; detection %d/%d; min raw p = %.3f\n",
              b, sum(d$adj_pvalue < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), nrow(d),
              sum(pa$fisher_adj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), nrow(pa),
              min(pa$fisher_p, na.rm = TRUE)))
}
```

So every treatment verdict is descriptive, coming from detection patterns
(HL-only / NL-only / both) rather than from a hypothesis test:

| Verdict | batch 1 | batch 2 |
|---|---|---|
| HL-leaning (detection) | 28 | 33 |
| NL-leaning (detection) | 3 | 4 |
| No clear NL/HL difference | 191 | 34 |

```{r verdicts}
n_verdicts <- function(batch) {
  v <- rd(batch, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_combined_verdict.csv")
  tibble(verdict = c("HL-leaning (detection)", "NL-leaning (detection)",
                     "no clear NL/HL difference"),
         n = as.integer(table(factor(v$verdict, levels = verdict))[verdict]))
}
left_join(mutate(n_verdicts(1), batch1 = n) |> select(-n),
          mutate(n_verdicts(2), batch2 = n) |> select(-n), by = "verdict")
```

Batch 2 looks more treatment-responsive (37 of 71 proteins vs 31 of 222), but
with 3 replicates its detection patterns are easier to produce by chance --- an
HL-exclusive call needs only 2/3 vs 0/3. The two batches are not comparable on
this axis.

All 38 batch-1 route B proteins and all 10 batch-2 route B proteins fell in "no
clear difference": they entered the comparison through enrichment over the
control, and nothing about them changed between treatments.

## Treatment-specific interactors

The detection arm splits the specific interactors by which treatment they were
seen in:

- **exclusive** --- reproducible in one treatment, absent from the other
  (`HL-exclusive`, `NL-exclusive`);
- **biased** --- seen in both, but in fewer replicates in one (`HL-biased`,
  `NL-biased`);
- **both treatments** --- equally reproducible in the two.

| Pattern | batch 1 (of 222) | batch 2 (of 71) |
|---|---|---|
| HL-exclusive | 28 | 33 |
| HL-biased | 77 | 7 |
| both treatments | 99 | 26 |
| NL-biased | 15 | 1 |
| NL-exclusive | 3 | 4 |

```{r treatment-specific}
n_pattern <- function(batch) {
  pa <- rd(batch, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_presence_absence.csv")
  lv <- c("HL-exclusive", "HL-biased", "both treatments", "NL-biased", "NL-exclusive")
  as.integer(table(factor(pa$pattern, levels = lv))[lv])
}
lvl <- c("HL-exclusive", "HL-biased", "both treatments", "NL-biased", "NL-exclusive")
tibble(pattern = lvl, batch1 = n_pattern(1), batch2 = n_pattern(2))
```

Both batches put a clear majority of treatment-specific proteins on the
high-light side: 28 vs 3 exclusive proteins in batch 1, 33 vs 4 in batch 2, and
the same direction for the biased proteins (77 vs 15, 7 vs 1). Batch 1's
exclusive calls are also stronger within a group: 23 of its 28 HL-exclusive
proteins were seen 3/4 and 5 were 4/4, whereas batch 2's are 23 at 2/3 and 10 at
3/3.

```{r exclusive-strength}
for (b in 1:2) {
  pa <- rd(b, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_presence_absence.csv")
  ex <- filter(pa, pattern %in% c("HL-exclusive", "NL-exclusive"))
  cat(sprintf("batch %d: %d exclusive proteins, replicate counts HL/NL:\n", b, nrow(ex)))
  print(table(HL = ex$det_HL, NL = ex$det_NL))
}
```

**The two batches share no exclusive protein at all** (0 HL-exclusive and 0
NL-exclusive in common), so there is no overlap to check agreement on. That,
plus a roughly threefold difference in the size of the specific set, means the
treatment-specific lists should be treated as batch-specific observations.

```{r exclusive-overlap}
ex_of <- function(batch) {
  pa <- rd(batch, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_presence_absence.csv")
  list(HL = pa$Protein.Group[pa$pattern == "HL-exclusive"],
       NL = pa$Protein.Group[pa$pattern == "NL-exclusive"])
}
e1 <- ex_of(1); e2 <- ex_of(2)
c(HL_exclusive_shared = length(intersect(e1$HL, e2$HL)),
  NL_exclusive_shared = length(intersect(e1$NL, e2$NL)))
```

Batch 2 looks about three times more treatment-specific (37 of 71 proteins,
52%) than batch 1 (31 of 222, 14%). That difference is best explained by the
rep 2/3 rule, not by biology: a 2/3 vs 0/3 pattern is easy to produce from
sampling, and with 3 replicates the detection test cannot reach significance
(minimum p = 0.10), so none of these calls is statistically supported in batch
2. Batch 1's 4/4-only exclusives are the strongest candidates on offer.

## Do the two batches agree?

Only 11 proteins are in both specific sets (211 batch-1 only, 60 batch-2 only),
so overlap cannot be assessed at scale.

```{r overlap}
s1 <- rd(1, "YAP1C_specific_interactors_broadened.csv")
s2 <- rd(2, "YAP1C_specific_interactors_broadened.csv")
cat("shared:", length(intersect(s1$Protein.Group, s2$Protein.Group)),
    "| batch 1 only:", length(setdiff(s1$Protein.Group, s2$Protein.Group)),
    "| batch 2 only:", length(setdiff(s2$Protein.Group, s1$Protein.Group)), "\n")
```

Among those 11:

- 8 agree on "no clear NL/HL difference"
- 2 are HL-leaning in batch 2 but not in batch 1
- 1 is HL-leaning in batch 1 (SAMC1) but not in batch 2

```{r verdict-agreement}
v1 <- rd(1, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_combined_verdict.csv")
v2 <- rd(2, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_combined_verdict.csv")
j <- inner_join(rename(v1, verdict1 = verdict) |> select(Protein.Group, Genes, verdict1),
                rename(v2, verdict2 = verdict) |> select(Protein.Group, verdict2),
                by = "Protein.Group")
print(table(j$verdict1, j$verdict2))
filter(j, verdict1 != verdict2)
```

The small overlap is the main caveat. Batch 1 identified 3624 interactors and
batch 2 1237, which is a much larger difference than a 4-vs-3 replicate change
would explain, so the two runs likely differ in depth or sample quality as well
as in size.

## Shared interactors: written to a file

The overlap is small enough to be worth reading protein by protein, so it is
written out alongside the batch results. One row per protein group that is a
specific interactor in **both** batches, with each batch's own columns kept
side by side (`_b1` and `_b2` suffixes) so nothing is merged or reinterpreted.

```{r shared-interactors}
dir.create(outdir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

v1 <- rd(1, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_combined_verdict.csv")
v2 <- rd(2, "YAP1C_NL_vs_HL_combined_verdict.csv")

keep <- c("Protein.Group", "Genes", "Protein.Names", "Description", "route",
          "qualifies_in", "tested_in", "det_HL", "det_NL", "pattern",
          "detection_class", "log2FC_HL_vs_NL", "adj_pvalue", "fisher_p", "verdict")

shared <- inner_join(
  select(v1, all_of(keep)) |> rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_b1"), -Protein.Group),
  select(v2, all_of(keep)) |> rename_with(~ paste0(.x, "_b2"), -Protein.Group),
  by = "Protein.Group") |>
  # one label per protein, preferring whichever batch mapped a gene symbol
  mutate(Genes = coalesce(Genes_b1, Genes_b2),
         verdict_agrees = verdict_b1 == verdict_b2) |>
  relocate(Genes, verdict_agrees, .after = Protein.Group) |>
  arrange(desc(verdict_agrees), Genes)

readr::write_csv(shared, file.path(outdir, "YAP1C_specific_interactors_shared_batch1_batch2.csv"))

cat("Shared specific interactors:", nrow(shared), "of",
    nrow(v1), "(batch 1) and", nrow(v2), "(batch 2)\n")
cat("Written to", file.path(outdir, "YAP1C_specific_interactors_shared_batch1_batch2.csv"), "\n")
shared
```

`verdict_agrees` is TRUE where both batches gave the protein the same treatment
verdict. A protein can be shared and still disagree, and those rows are the ones
worth looking at by hand.

## Known gaps in batch 2

- The Ensembl peptide-ID lookup returned no mappings, so protein groups fell back
  to UniProt accessions and `uniprot_to_ensembl_peptide.csv` was not written.
- Because of that, no TAIR loci were found and the whole GO section was skipped:
  `YAP1C_GO_enrichment.csv` is missing. Batch 1's GO table exists and cannot be
  reproduced for batch 2 until the mapping is fixed.
- The 3 heatmap SVGs in batch 2 were previously written to the project root; they
  now go to `output_batch2/results`.

## Bottom line

Both batches give the same qualitative answer: the specific YAP1C interactors
are dominated by proteins absent from the control, and high light does not
change their capture by intensity. Batch 2 is too small, and its detection test
too underpowered, to confirm or contradict the few treatment-leaning proteins
batch 1 reported; treat batch 2 as supporting evidence for the identity of
interactors, not for their light response.
